# The Differential Equations of Living Systems {#ch1}

```{r ch1-setup}
# Chapter 1 Setup
# All packages and global settings for this chapter.
# This chunk is self-contained — it does not depend on any prior chapter.

library(tidyverse)
library(deSolve)
library(patchwork)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Source Serif 4") +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(family = "Raleway", face = "plain",
                                      size = 14, margin = margin(b = 8)),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(family = "Source Serif 4", size = 11,
                                      color = "#555555", margin = margin(b = 12)),
      axis.title       = element_text(family = "Source Serif 4", size = 10),
      legend.position  = "bottom",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#FAFAF7", color = NA)
    )
)

palette_ch1 <- c(
  prey        = "#2D5F8A",
  predator    = "#8A4A2D",
  susceptible = "#2D5F8A",
  infectious  = "#C0392B",
  recovered   = "#27AE60"
)
```

A population of rabbits with unlimited food grows exponentially. Or does it? After all, the fox population grows with it — and then the rabbits decline — and then the foxes, deprived of prey, decline in turn — and then the rabbits recover. We expect growth to continue or stop; not to cycle. We expect an epidemic to burn through everyone it can reach. These expectations are wrong, and they are wrong in the same way: something in the process is feeding back on the conditions of its own continuation. [@Lotka1925; @Volterra1926] Human intuition handles feedback poorly.

The differential equation is the instrument built for exactly this. The state determines the rate; the rate changes the state; the new state determines a new rate — the equation captures this self-referential loop and makes it tractable.

Alas, familiar equations, over time, render their assumptions invisible. The predator-prey model and the epidemic model are a century old; the choices embedded in their functional forms have had that long to become invisible. What is hiding in those forms — and what it costs to have those things hidden — is what the rest of this course is about.

For statisticians, the central question is not whether agent-based models are more realistic but rather: which distinctions does the inference require? If heterogeneity, contact dependence, discreteness, or temporal ordering affect the phenomenon, then an aggregate model that omits them is not merely simpler. It belongs to a model family in which those distinctions cannot affect the answer.

## Predators, Prey, and the Geometry of Cycles {#sec-lv}

Begin with the prey. Absent predators, a prey population grows at a rate proportional to its size — each individual produces offspring at the same per-capita rate $\alpha$, and the population is not resource-constrained. This gives the exponential growth term $\alpha N$. Predators, absent prey, decline at a per-capita rate $\gamma$ — they die without food. These are the uncoupled dynamics: rabbits grow, foxes die.

Coupling enters through encounters. A predator that encounters a prey individual kills it with some probability; the encounter benefits the predator. The rate at which these encounters occur is proportional to the product $NP$. This deserves a moment's attention before the equation appears. The product $NP$ says that every predator is equally likely to encounter every prey individual: if there are twice as many prey, encounters double; if there are twice as many predators, encounters double. The encounter rate is the product of the two abundances, multiplied by a rate constant $\beta$ that converts encounters into kills.

$$\frac{dN}{dt} = \alpha N - \beta N P$$

$$\frac{dP}{dt} = \delta N P - \gamma P$$

The parameter $\alpha$ is the prey birth rate; $\beta$ is the predation rate coefficient — the probability per unit time per predator-prey pair that an encounter results in a kill; $\delta$ is the conversion efficiency, the rate at which prey consumed is converted into predator offspring; $\gamma$ is the predator death rate. Four parameters. Two equations. A complete description of a world with two species and one interaction. [@Lotka1925; @Volterra1926ita]

::: {.activitybox data-latex="true"}
**Activity — Predict Before Computing (10 minutes)**

Starting from $N(0)=10$ prey and $P(0)=5$ predators, sketch both populations through time. Mark which population peaks first and decide whether the cycles grow, shrink, or remain constant. Then compare sketches with a partner and identify the assumption doing the most work in your prediction. Do not solve the equations before committing to a sketch.
:::

The nullclines — the curves along which each population is momentarily stationary — divide the phase plane into four regions. The prey nullcline $dN/dt = 0$ requires either $N = 0$ or $P = \alpha/\beta$: the prey population is constant when the predator population is exactly $\alpha/\beta$, regardless of how many prey there are. The predator nullcline $dP/dt = 0$ requires either $P = 0$ or $N = \gamma/\delta$: predators are stationary when prey are at exactly $\gamma/\delta$. The nontrivial equilibrium is the crossing point: $N^* = \gamma/\delta$, $P^* = \alpha/\beta$.

The trajectories are closed orbits around this equilibrium — neither converging to it nor expanding away. The system cycles forever without damping or growth. This is the pendulum that never loses energy, a machine that returns to any given state without ever simplifying toward rest. It is geometrically beautiful and physically strange. A physicist would say the system is conservative — it has a constant of motion, a quantity that is preserved along every trajectory. Volterra showed that $\delta N - \gamma \ln N + \beta P - \alpha \ln P$ is constant along solutions of the system [@Volterra1926ita]. The orbits are the level curves of this conserved quantity.

Each initial condition $(N_0, P_0)$ selects a particular orbit, and the system follows that orbit infinitely. The orbits nest. The central equilibrium point is not a fixed point in the attracting sense — it is surrounded by a continuous family of periodic orbits which differ in amplitude of the same cycle. The phase plane is therefore not a diagram of what the system tends toward; it is a diagram of what the system does forever.

```{r ch1-lv-timeseries, fig.cap="Lotka-Volterra predator-prey dynamics. Prey (blue) and predator (brown) populations cycle indefinitely. Parameters: $\\alpha = 0.8$, $\\beta = 0.4$, $\\delta = 0.3$, $\\gamma = 0.6$."}
# Lotka-Volterra ODE system
# set.seed not required here — deSolve is deterministic
lv_params <- c(alpha = 0.8, beta = 0.4, delta = 0.3, gamma = 0.6)
lv_state  <- c(N = 10, P = 5)

lv_ode <- function(t, state, params) {
  with(as.list(c(state, params)), {
    dN <- alpha * N - beta * N * P
    dP <- delta * N * P - gamma * P
    list(c(dN, dP))
  })
}

times_lv <- seq(0, 50, by = 0.1)
lv_out   <- ode(y = lv_state, times = times_lv, func = lv_ode, parms = lv_params)

lv_df <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(lv_out)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(N, P), names_to = "species", values_to = "population") %>%
  mutate(species = recode(species, N = "prey", P = "predator"))

ggplot(lv_df, aes(x = time, y = population, color = species)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = palette_ch1[c("prey", "predator")],
    labels = c("prey" = "Prey (N)", "predator" = "Predator (P)")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "Lotka-Volterra: population time series",
    subtitle = expression(alpha == 0.8 ~ "," ~ beta == 0.4 ~ "," ~ delta == 0.3 ~ "," ~ gamma == 0.6),
    x        = "Time",
    y        = "Population",
    color    = NULL
  )
```

```{r ch1-lv-phase, fig.cap="Phase portrait of Lotka-Volterra dynamics. Each curve is a closed orbit corresponding to a different initial condition. The system returns to each point on a given orbit with exact periodicity."}
# Phase portrait: multiple initial conditions
# The system is deterministic; no seed needed
initial_conditions <- list(
  c(N = 10, P = 5),
  c(N = 15, P = 4),
  c(N = 8,  P = 7),
  c(N = 20, P = 3),
  c(N = 6,  P = 9)
)

orbit_df <- map_dfr(
  seq_along(initial_conditions),
  function(i) {
    out <- ode(
      y     = initial_conditions[[i]],
      times = seq(0, 80, by = 0.05),
      func  = lv_ode,
      parms = lv_params
    )
    as_tibble(as.data.frame(out)) %>%
      mutate(orbit = factor(i))
  }
)

# Equilibrium point
N_star <- lv_params["gamma"] / lv_params["delta"]
P_star <- lv_params["alpha"] / lv_params["beta"]

ggplot(orbit_df, aes(x = N, y = P, color = orbit)) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  annotate("point", x = N_star, y = P_star, size = 3, color = "#1C1C1E") +
  annotate("text", x = N_star + 0.4, y = P_star + 0.3,
           label = "Equilibrium", family = "Source Serif 4", size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colorRampPalette(c("#2D5F8A", "#8A4A2D"))(5)) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Lotka-Volterra: phase portrait",
    subtitle = "Five initial conditions, each tracing a closed orbit",
    x = "Prey population (N)",
    y = "Predator population (P)"
  )
```

## The Mean-Field Assumption {#sec-meanfield}

Within the product term $\beta NP$, hides an assumption in plain sight.

The expression says that the rate of predator-prey encounters is proportional to the product of population sizes. For this to hold, every predator must be equally likely to encounter every prey individual at every moment. The population is perfectly mixed. There is no space and thus no location. Individuals have neither territories, nor persistent relationships. There are no dense patches and no empty expanses. The assumption is that the spatial arrangement is irrelevant because mixing is instantaneous and complete.

We call this the mean-field assumption, borrowing the name from physics, where it appears in the analysis of magnetic systems: the effective field experienced by any one particle is the mean field produced by all the others, rather than the specific field produced by its actual neighbors [@Sethna2021]. In population ecology it enters through the functional form of the interaction term — unstated in most presentations of Lotka-Volterra, embedded in the mathematics rather than declared before the equations. The product $NP$ is one modeling choice among others; it is the one that assumes perfect mixing.

The mean-field assumption is a structural model-family choice: it selects the class of models governed by mass-action kinetics, excluding all others — network models, spatial models, individual-based models — prior to any data. The product $NP$ is not a parameter to be estimated. It is the choice of family, and that choice determines what phenomena the family can express. Structured populations, spatial aggregations, social networks among individuals, heterogeneous encounter rates. These are not in the family.

That family choice is simultaneously a choice about temporal resolution. The ODE family is defined in continuous time — formally, the limit as the time step shrinks to zero. But the interaction term $\beta NP$ is appropriate only when the observation interval is coarse enough for the law of large numbers to operate across interactions within each step. At fine enough temporal resolution the family is misspecified: in any given instant most individuals are not contacting most others, and the product term misrepresents the actual contact process. The mean-field ODE is the right family at temporal resolutions coarse enough for spatial averaging to hold within each step. Whether that condition is satisfied is an empirical question about the system's contact dynamics — not a modeling convenience.

The clean closed-orbit result depends on this assumption. When real predator-prey systems fail to cycle as neatly as the model predicts, the mean-field assumption may be the culprit. Its most important consequences, however, will not come into view until the contrast with agent-based models is drawn.

## Epidemics and the Threshold Phenomenon {#sec-sir}

The same assumption appears in epidemic modeling, in precisely the same place, governing a different interaction.

Consider a closed population of $N$ individuals. Each is in one of three states: Susceptible, Infectious, or Recovered (and immune). Infectious individuals shed pathogen; susceptible individuals become infected upon exposure. The rate at which susceptible individuals encounter infectious ones is proportional to $SI$ — the number of susceptibles times the number of infecteds, multiplied by a rate constant $\beta$. Recovery occurs at per-capita rate $\gamma$. [@Kermack1927]

$$\frac{dS}{dt} = -\beta S I$$

$$\frac{dI}{dt} = \beta S I - \gamma I$$

$$\frac{dR}{dt} = \gamma I$$

The mean-field assumption is here again: the contact rate is proportional to the product $SI$, which assumes that every susceptible individual is equally likely to contact every infectious individual. Human contact, of course, is not structured this way. People have households, workplaces, social networks — structures that make some contacts far more probable than others. The SIR model, like Lotka-Volterra, assumes this structure away.

From the sign of $dI/dt$ at the start of an epidemic, when $S \approx N$:

$$\frac{dI}{dt}\bigg|_{t=0} \approx I(\beta N - \gamma) = I \cdot \gamma\left(\frac{\beta N}{\gamma} - 1\right)$$

The epidemic grows if $\beta N / \gamma > 1$ and dies out if $\beta N / \gamma < 1$. The quantity $\mathcal{R}_0 = \beta N / \gamma$ is the basic reproduction number: the expected number of secondary infections produced by a single infectious individual in a fully susceptible population [@Kermack1927; @Hethcote2000]. It is not a numerical fact to memorize. It is a structural consequence of the model — a ratio between the transmission term and the recovery term, visible directly in the algebra. The epidemic threshold at $\mathcal{R}_0 = 1$ is where the production of new infections exactly balances the removal of current ones.

In the years since 2020 many of us have thought more about this model than we ever ancitipated. The herd immunity threshold, the effect of contact reduction, the role of $\mathcal{R}_0$ in policy discussions — these became household concepts in a span of weeks. What remained, for the most part, unstated in those discussions was the mean-field assumption underlying the standard SIR framework: that the contact structure of the population could be adequately represented by the product $SI$, ignoring the network topology that governs who actually contacts whom.

```{r ch1-sir-base, fig.cap="SIR epidemic dynamics. The epidemic rises, peaks when the susceptible pool is depleted sufficiently, and declines. The herd immunity threshold is reached when enough individuals have recovered that $\\mathcal{R}_0 S/N < 1$."}
# SIR ODE implementation
sir_params <- c(beta = 0.0003, gamma = 0.1)
sir_state  <- c(S = 999, I = 1, R = 0)
N_pop      <- sum(sir_state)

# R0 under these parameters
R0_base <- sir_params["beta"] * N_pop / sir_params["gamma"]

sir_ode <- function(t, state, params) {
  with(as.list(c(state, params)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I
    dI <-  beta * S * I - gamma * I
    dR <-  gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}

times_sir <- seq(0, 200, by = 0.5)
sir_out   <- ode(y = sir_state, times = times_sir, func = sir_ode, parms = sir_params)

sir_df <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(sir_out)) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(S, I, R), names_to = "compartment", values_to = "count") %>%
  mutate(
    compartment = factor(
      compartment,
      levels = c("S", "I", "R"),
      labels = c("susceptible", "infectious", "recovered")
    )
  )

ggplot(sir_df, aes(x = time, y = count, color = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = palette_ch1[c("susceptible", "infectious", "recovered")]
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "SIR epidemic dynamics",
    subtitle = bquote(beta == .(sir_params["beta"]) ~ "," ~
                      gamma == .(sir_params["gamma"]) ~ "," ~
                      R[0] == .(round(R0_base, 2))),
    x        = "Time",
    y        = "Count",
    color    = NULL
  )
```

```{r ch1-sir-sweep, fig.cap="SIR epidemic curves across values of $\\mathcal{R}_0$. Each curve shows the infectious compartment $I(t)$ for a different transmission rate. The epidemic threshold at $\\mathcal{R}_0 = 1$ is visible: below it, no outbreak occurs; above it, epidemic size grows with $\\mathcal{R}_0$."}
# Parameter sweep over R0
# Vary beta to produce different R0 values; gamma and N fixed

set.seed(2025)  # seed for reproducibility; results are deterministic here, but good practice

R0_values <- c(0.8, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0)
gamma_fixed <- 0.1
N_fixed     <- 1000

sweep_df <- map_dfr(R0_values, function(r0) {
  beta_val <- r0 * gamma_fixed / N_fixed
  params_i <- c(beta = beta_val, gamma = gamma_fixed)
  state_i  <- c(S = N_fixed - 10, I = 10, R = 0)
  out_i    <- ode(y = state_i, times = seq(0, 250, by = 0.5),
                  func = sir_ode, parms = params_i)
  as_tibble(as.data.frame(out_i)) %>%
    mutate(R0 = r0) %>%
    select(time, I, R0)
})

ggplot(sweep_df, aes(x = time, y = I, color = factor(R0), group = factor(R0))) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = colorRampPalette(c("#AED6F1", "#C0392B"))(length(R0_values)),
    name   = expression(R[0])
  ) +
  labs(
    title = expression("SIR epidemic curves across values of" ~ R[0]),
    x     = "Time",
    y     = "Infectious individuals (I)"
  )
```

## What the Language Can Say {#sec-ch1-language}

A differential equation governing $dN/dt$ must treat $N$ as something smooth enough to differentiate: a real number rather than a count. The prey population $N = 3.7$ is as valid a model state as $N = 37$ or $N = 370$. The formalism is not approximating a discrete reality; it is positing a different one. Individuals are absent. Only totals exist.

From the decision to track totals, the rest follows by a logical chain with no exits. A total has no internal distribution: the ODE has only $N$, so all prey individuals must be identical — same predation risk, same birth rate. A real fox population contains young and old, healthy and sick, bold hunters and timid ones. The ODE contains none of this.

Identical individuals interacting through their totals: the mean-field assumption, arrived at not by declaration but by consequence. If all prey individuals are equivalent, the encounter rate is proportional to $N$, independently of position or history. The product $\beta NP$ follows immediately — a consequence of the prior two choices, not a third independent assumption. Space disappears because individuals have no positions; history disappears because two numbers are all the state there is.

These choices have been scientifically productive for over a century. Lotka-Volterra was formulated in the 1920s [@Lotka1925; @Volterra1926]; SIR was published in 1927 by Kermack and McKendrick [@Kermack1927]. The models have generated real insight into predator-prey dynamics, epidemic thresholds, herd immunity. The chain — continuity, homogeneity, mean-field, no position, no history — was forged in a few equations and has persisted every since. 
The product term $\beta NP$ is this commitment. When it fits, the model is the right instrument. When it fails, the model gives precise answers — about an imaginary world.

# Agents, Networks, and the Geometry of Interaction {#ch2}

```{r ch2-setup}
# Chapter 2 Setup
# Self-contained — does not depend on Chapter 1.

library(tidyverse)
library(deSolve)
library(igraph)
library(tidygraph)
library(ggraph)
library(gganimate)
library(patchwork)

theme_set(
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Source Serif 4") +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(family = "Raleway", face = "plain",
                                      size = 14, margin = margin(b = 8)),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(family = "Source Serif 4", size = 11,
                                      color = "#555555", margin = margin(b = 12)),
      axis.title       = element_text(family = "Source Serif 4", size = 10),
      legend.position  = "bottom",
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "#FAFAF7", color = NA)
    )
)

palette_ch2 <- c(
  prey        = "#2D5F8A",
  predator    = "#8A4A2D",
  susceptible = "#2D5F8A",
  infectious  = "#C0392B",
  recovered   = "#27AE60"
)

# ODE parameters derived from the ABM individual-level rates:
#   alpha = p_birth = 0.15   (per-capita prey birth rate per step)
#   gamma = p_death = 0.10   (per-capita predator death rate per step)
#   beta  = p_kill  = 0.00375 (kill probability per predator-prey pair per step)
#   delta = p_kill * p_convert = 0.00375 * 0.267 ≈ 0.001 (predator birth rate)
# Equilibrium: N* = gamma/delta = 100, P* = alpha/beta = 40.
# Starting at (N=200, P=40): N is above N*, P is at P*, so P rises first
# while N stays near 200, then both oscillate. Period ≈ 51 steps.
lv_params_ch2 <- c(alpha = 0.15, beta = 0.00375, delta = 0.001, gamma = 0.10)
lv_ode_ch2 <- function(t, state, params) {
  with(as.list(c(state, params)), {
    dN <- alpha * N - beta * N * P
    dP <- delta * N * P - gamma * P
    list(c(dN, dP))
  })
}

sir_params_ch2 <- c(beta = 0.0003, gamma = 0.1)
sir_ode_ch2 <- function(t, state, params) {
  with(as.list(c(state, params)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I
    dI <-  beta * S * I - gamma * I
    dR <-  gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}
```

## What Is an Agent? {#sec-agents}

The ODE compresses a population of a hundred rabbits to the number 100 — a total that absorbs their individual differences into a single quantity. The agent-based model takes those hundred rabbits seriously as a hundred rabbits. Each has a state. Each has a neighborhood: the set of other agents it can actually interact with at this time step. [@EpsteinAxtell1996] The moment a neighborhood is anything other than "the entire population, uniformly weighted," the mean-field assumption fails and the right answer falls outside the model's language.

Give an agent a neighborhood smaller than the full population, and you give the model a new kind of sentence. The neighborhood can be spatial — the eight cells surrounding a position on a grid. It can be social — the edges of a contact network.

## An Agent-Based Lotka-Volterra {#sec-abm-lv}

The biology is unchanged. Prey reproduce, predators hunt, predators die — the same rules as the differential equations. What changes is the substrate: a population of discrete individuals rather than a continuous quantity.

Each individual is a row in a `tibble` carrying an identifier, a type (prey or predator), and an alive status. At each discrete time step: each surviving prey reproduces with probability $p_\text{birth}$; each predator independently encounters each prey individual with probability $p_\text{kill}$, killing it on contact; each kill produces a new predator with probability $p_\text{convert}$; each predator dies independently with probability $p_\text{death}$. The parameters map directly onto the ODE: $p_\text{birth} = \alpha$, $p_\text{kill} = \beta$, $p_\text{kill} \times p_\text{convert} = \delta$, $p_\text{death} = \gamma$ — the same rates, now governing discrete individuals rather than continuous quantities.

```{r ch2-abm-lv-functions}
# Agent-based Lotka-Volterra
# Population represented as a tibble with one row per individual

init_lv_abm <- function(n_prey, n_pred) {
  # Initialize population with prey and predator agents
  bind_rows(
    tibble(id = seq_len(n_prey),           type = "prey",     alive = TRUE),
    tibble(id = seq_len(n_pred) + n_prey,  type = "predator", alive = TRUE)
  )
}

step_lv_abm <- function(pop, p_birth = 0.15, p_kill = 0.00375, p_convert = 0.267,
                        p_death = 0.10, max_pop = 5000L) {
  # One time step of the agent-based LV model.
  # Each predator independently encounters each prey with probability p_kill
  # per pair per step — the direct individual-level interpretation of the
  # beta*N*P term. Expected kills per step = p_kill * N * P = beta * N * P.
  # Each kill produces a new predator with probability p_convert, so
  # delta = p_kill * p_convert in the ODE.
  prey  <- filter(pop, type == "prey",     alive)
  preds <- filter(pop, type == "predator", alive)
  N     <- nrow(prey)
  P     <- nrow(preds)
  max_id <- max(pop$id, 0L)

  # --- Prey reproduction ---
  # max_pop is a safety cap against runaway growth in low-predation phases.
  n_born <- if (N >= max_pop) 0L else rbinom(1, N, p_birth)
  new_prey <- if (n_born > 0) {
    tibble(id = seq_len(n_born) + max_id, type = "prey", alive = TRUE)
  } else {
    tibble(id = integer(), type = character(), alive = logical())
  }
  max_id <- max_id + n_born

  # --- Predator-prey encounters ---
  # Each predator kills Binomial(N, p_kill) prey independently.
  # Deduplication ensures each prey dies at most once per step.
  dead_prey_ids <- integer(0)
  new_pred_rows <- tibble(id = integer(), type = character(), alive = logical())

  if (N > 0 && P > 0) {
    kills_per_pred <- rbinom(P, N, p_kill)
    all_kills <- unlist(lapply(kills_per_pred[kills_per_pred > 0], function(k) {
      slice_sample(prey, n = min(k, N))$id
    }))
    dead_prey_ids <- unique(all_kills)
    n_kills_total <- length(dead_prey_ids)

    if (n_kills_total > 0) {
      n_new_pred <- rbinom(1L, n_kills_total, p_convert)
      if (n_new_pred > 0) {
        new_pred_rows <- tibble(
          id    = seq_len(n_new_pred) + max_id,
          type  = "predator",
          alive = TRUE
        )
        max_id <- max_id + n_new_pred
      }
    }
  }

  # --- Predator natural death ---
  dead_pred_ids <- preds$id[rbinom(nrow(preds), 1, p_death) == 1]

  pop_surviving <- pop %>%
    mutate(alive = alive & !(id %in% c(dead_prey_ids, dead_pred_ids))) %>%
    filter(alive)

  bind_rows(pop_surviving, new_prey, new_pred_rows)
}

run_lv_abm <- function(T = 200, n_prey = 100, n_pred = 20, seed = 42, ...) {
  # Run the ABM for T steps and return a tidy time series
  set.seed(seed)  # seed for reproducibility; change to explore stochastic variation
  pop <- init_lv_abm(n_prey, n_pred)

  map_dfr(0:T, function(tt) {
    if (tt > 0) pop <<- step_lv_abm(pop, ...)
    tibble(
      t        = tt,
      prey     = sum(pop$type == "prey"),
      predator = sum(pop$type == "predator")
    )
  })
}
```

```{r ch2-abm-lv-reduction, fig.cap="Ten stochastic ABM runs (translucent lines) overlaid on the corresponding mean-field ODE solution (solid lines). For a suitably scaled, density-dependent process with random mixing, the normalized ABM trajectory approaches the ODE over finite time horizons as population size grows."}
# Run 10 ABM replications with a large population
# Each run uses a different seed to show stochastic variation

set.seed(2025)  # master seed for reproducibility

n_reps   <- 10
T_run    <- 300   # matches slides; covers several LV cycles
n_prey0  <- 60
n_pred0  <- 15

abm_runs <- map_dfr(1:n_reps, function(rep) {
  run_lv_abm(T = T_run, n_prey = n_prey0, n_pred = n_pred0, seed = rep,
             p_birth = 0.15, p_kill = 0.00375, p_convert = 0.267,
             p_death = 0.10) %>%
    mutate(rep = rep)
})

# ODE solution for comparison — scaled to the same initial conditions
ode_state_ch2 <- c(N = n_prey0, P = n_pred0)
ode_out_ch2   <- ode(
  y     = ode_state_ch2,
  times = seq(0, T_run, by = 1),
  func  = lv_ode_ch2,
  parms = lv_params_ch2
)
ode_df_ch2 <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(ode_out_ch2)) %>%
  rename(t = time, prey = N, predator = P)

# Tidy ABM runs for plotting
abm_long <- abm_runs %>%
  pivot_longer(c(prey, predator), names_to = "species", values_to = "count")

ode_long <- ode_df_ch2 %>%
  pivot_longer(c(prey, predator), names_to = "species", values_to = "count")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = abm_long,
    aes(x = t, y = count, color = species, group = interaction(rep, species)),
    alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = ode_long,
    aes(x = t, y = count, color = species),
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = palette_ch2[c("prey", "predator")],
    labels = c("prey" = "Prey", "predator" = "Predator")
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "ABM replicates vs. ODE solution",
    subtitle = "Translucent lines: 10 stochastic ABM runs. Solid lines: ODE. Initial N = 60 prey, 15 predators.",
    x        = "Time step",
    y        = "Population count",
    color    = NULL
  )
```

In this construction, stochastic variation narrows around the ODE trajectory as population size grows. The limiting statement requires more than a large, randomly mixed population: the transition rates must have the density-dependent scaling that generates the stated drift, and convergence is ordinarily asserted for normalized trajectories over finite time intervals [@Kurtz1970; @Kurtz1978]. Random mixing is therefore one structural condition in this example, not by itself a complete convergence theorem.

Now reduce the population.

```{r ch2-abm-extinction, fig.cap="Finite-time extinction in a small stochastic population. The deterministic ODE remains positive and orbits indefinitely from the same positive initial condition; ABM runs can hit zero, after which extinction is absorbing."}
# Small-population ABM: extinction is possible
set.seed(2025)  # reproducibility

n_reps_small <- 15
T_small      <- 150
n_prey_small <- 20   # small enough for demographic stochasticity to matter
n_pred_small <- 8

abm_small <- map_dfr(1:n_reps_small, function(rep) {
  run_lv_abm(
    T         = T_small,
    n_prey    = n_prey_small,
    n_pred    = n_pred_small,
    seed      = rep + 100,
    p_birth   = 0.15,
    p_kill    = 0.00375,
    p_convert = 0.267,
    p_death   = 0.10
  ) %>%
    mutate(rep = rep)
})

# ODE solution with the same (small) initial conditions
ode_small_state <- c(N = n_prey_small, P = n_pred_small)
ode_small_out   <- ode(
  y     = ode_small_state,
  times = seq(0, T_small, by = 1),
  func  = lv_ode_ch2,
  parms = lv_params_ch2
)
ode_small_df <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(ode_small_out)) %>%
  rename(t = time, prey = N, predator = P) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(prey, predator), names_to = "species", values_to = "count")

abm_small_long <- abm_small %>%
  pivot_longer(c(prey, predator), names_to = "species", values_to = "count")

# Count extinctions
extinction_count <- abm_small %>%
  group_by(rep) %>%
  summarise(
    prey_extinct     = any(prey == 0),
    predator_extinct = any(predator == 0)
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_any_extinct = sum(prey_extinct | predator_extinct)
  ) %>%
  pull(n_any_extinct)

# Set ylim just above the peaks of the well-behaved (periodic/extinct) runs.
# Diverging runs exceed this limit and are clipped; noted in the text below.
run_peaks <- abm_small_long %>%
  group_by(rep, species) %>%
  summarise(peak = max(count), .groups = "drop")
ylim_cap <- quantile(run_peaks$peak, 0.80) * 1.05

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = abm_small_long,
    aes(x = t, y = count, color = species, group = interaction(rep, species)),
    alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = ode_small_df,
    aes(x = t, y = count, color = species),
    linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = palette_ch2[c("prey", "predator")],
    labels = c("prey" = "Prey", "predator" = "Predator")
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, ylim_cap)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Small-population ABM: extinction events",
    subtitle = paste0(
      extinction_count, " of ", n_reps_small,
      " runs reach extinction. Dashed: ODE (cycles forever). N0 = ",
      n_prey_small, " prey, ", n_pred_small, " predators."
    ),
    x     = "Time step",
    y     = "Population count",
    color = NULL
  )
```

The ODE orbits forever. For the Lotka-Volterra system with positive initial conditions, the positive quadrant is invariant: trajectories do not reach zero. The ABM can fall to zero because it represents discrete individuals: when the last prey individual dies, the population is extinguished, and that is a state from which there is no return. The phenomenon of extinction — one of the most consequential events in population biology — has no representation in the ODE's state space: the ODE's variables are real-valued and positive, and zero is not an absorbing state. [@Lande1993]

A minority of runs go the other direction entirely: demographic stochasticity amplifies a favorable initial sequence and the population explodes before the predator response can stabilize it. Those runs exceed the figure's y-axis limit and are clipped — the upper face of small-number noise, and equally outside the ODE's representational range.

## An Agent-Based SIR {#sec-abm-sir}

### Random Mixing {#sec-abm-sir-random}

To begin with as simpler a departure from the ODE as possible, suppose each infectious agent contacts random members of the population at each step — the contact structure is still fully mixed, still mass-action — but the population is now a collection of persons rather than a continuous quantity. The mean-field assumption survives the move to discrete individuals. The point is to show that the individual-based model recovers the ODE when the assumption holds, then ask what happens when it doesn't. So far, only the implementation has changed.

```{r ch2-abm-sir-functions}
# Agent-based SIR with random mixing
# Each infectious agent contacts a random subset of the population at each step

run_sir_abm_random <- function(N = 500, I0 = 5, p_infect = 0.05,
                                p_recover = 0.1, contacts_per_step = 5,
                                T = 150, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)  # seed for reproducibility; change to explore variation

  agents <- tibble(
    id    = seq_len(N),
    state = c(rep("I", I0), rep("S", N - I0))
  )

  map_dfr(0:T, function(tt) {
    if (tt > 0) {
      infected_ids <- agents$id[agents$state == "I"]

      # Each infected agent makes contacts with random agents
      new_infected <- map(infected_ids, function(inf_id) {
        contacts           <- sample(setdiff(agents$id, inf_id),
                                     min(contacts_per_step, N - 1),
                                     replace = FALSE)
        suscept_contacts   <- contacts[agents$state[contacts] == "S"]
        if (length(suscept_contacts) == 0) return(integer(0))
        suscept_contacts[rbinom(length(suscept_contacts), 1, p_infect) == 1]
      }) %>%
        unlist() %>%
        unique()

      # Recovery
      recovering <- infected_ids[rbinom(length(infected_ids), 1, p_recover) == 1]

      agents <<- agents %>%
        mutate(state = case_when(
          id %in% new_infected & state == "S" ~ "I",
          id %in% recovering                  ~ "R",
          TRUE                                ~ state
        ))
    }

    tibble(
      t = tt,
      S = sum(agents$state == "S"),
      I = sum(agents$state == "I"),
      R = sum(agents$state == "R")
    )
  })
}
```

```{r ch2-sir-random-vs-ode, fig.cap="Agent-based SIR under random mixing (N = 500, 10 replicates shown as translucent lines) vs. ODE solution (solid lines). Convergence to the ODE is visible: the individual-based model recovers the mean-field dynamics when contacts are drawn uniformly from the population."}
set.seed(2025)

N_sir_compare <- 500
I0_compare    <- 5

# Run ABM replicates
sir_abm_runs <- map_dfr(1:10, function(rep) {
  run_sir_abm_random(
    N = N_sir_compare, I0 = I0_compare,
    p_infect = 0.05, p_recover = 0.1, contacts_per_step = 5,
    T = 150, seed = rep + 200
  ) %>%
    mutate(rep = rep)
})

# ODE comparison — match approximate R0
# R0 ≈ (p_infect * contacts_per_step) / p_recover  (rough approximation)
approx_R0  <- (0.05 * 5) / 0.1
beta_match <- approx_R0 * 0.1 / N_sir_compare

sir_ode_state <- c(S = N_sir_compare - I0_compare, I = I0_compare, R = 0)
sir_ode_out   <- ode(
  y     = sir_ode_state,
  times = seq(0, 150, by = 0.5),
  func  = sir_ode_ch2,
  parms = c(beta = beta_match, gamma = 0.1)
)
sir_ode_compare <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(sir_ode_out)) %>%
  rename(t = time)

sir_abm_long <- sir_abm_runs %>%
  pivot_longer(c(S, I, R), names_to = "compartment", values_to = "count") %>%
  mutate(compartment = factor(compartment, levels = c("S", "I", "R"),
                              labels = c("susceptible", "infectious", "recovered")))

sir_ode_long <- sir_ode_compare %>%
  pivot_longer(c(S, I, R), names_to = "compartment", values_to = "count") %>%
  mutate(compartment = factor(compartment, levels = c("S", "I", "R"),
                              labels = c("susceptible", "infectious", "recovered")))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = sir_abm_long,
    aes(x = t, y = count, color = compartment,
        group = interaction(rep, compartment)),
    alpha = 0.2, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = sir_ode_long,
    aes(x = t, y = count, color = compartment),
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = palette_ch2[c("susceptible", "infectious", "recovered")]
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "ABM SIR (random mixing) vs. ODE",
    subtitle = paste0("N = ", N_sir_compare, "; 10 stochastic replicates (faint) vs. ODE (solid)"),
    x        = "Time step",
    y        = "Count",
    color    = NULL
  )
```

### Network SIR {#sec-abm-sir-network}

Now suppose the agents are connected in a social network; families, schools, workplaces etc. We will consider two network models. 

::: {.activitybox data-latex="true"}
**Activity — Model Autopsy (15 minutes)**

For each question below, name the distinction the model must retain, decide whether a mean-field SIR can answer it, and identify any missing state or structure.

1. What will the epidemic peak be?
2. Who should receive a limited vaccine supply?
3. Does clustering protect part of the population?
4. How variable are outcomes across outbreaks?

Separate a question the model answers poorly from one it cannot express. Prepare one case to defend in a sentence.
:::

```{r ch2-networks-generate}
set.seed(2025)  # reproducibility for network generation

N_net   <- 500
avg_deg <- 6   # target mean degree

# Erdős-Rényi: edges placed independently with fixed probability
# Mean degree = p * (N - 1) ≈ avg_deg
g_er <- igraph::erdos.renyi.game(N_net, p = avg_deg / (N_net - 1))

# Barabási-Albert: preferential attachment produces a heavy-tailed degree distribution
# m = edges added per new node; mean degree ≈ 2m
g_ba <- igraph::sample_pa(N_net, m = avg_deg / 2, directed = FALSE)

# Verify mean degrees are comparable
mean_deg_er <- mean(igraph::degree(g_er))
mean_deg_ba <- mean(igraph::degree(g_ba))
```

These networks have comparable mean degree — each individual is connected to roughly the same number of others on average. What differs is the distribution of that degree. The Erdős-Rényi graph is the random graph: each pair of nodes is connected independently with fixed probability, and the degree distribution is approximately Poisson [@ErdosRenyi1959; @ErdosRenyi1960]. In a Poisson degree distribution, most nodes have degree close to the mean; there are no hubs. The Barabási-Albert graph grows by preferential attachment — new nodes attach to existing nodes in proportion to their current degree, and rich nodes get richer [@Barabasi1999]. The result is a scale-free degree distribution: most nodes have few connections, but a small number of hubs have very many. These hubs do not appear in an Erdős-Rényi network with the same mean degree.

```{r ch2-network-sir-function}
# Network SIR: infection spreads along edges
# Nodes are infected by each infected neighbor independently with probability p_infect

run_network_sir <- function(g, I0 = 5, p_infect = 0.05, p_recover = 0.1,
                              T = 100, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)  # seed for reproducibility

  N     <- igraph::vcount(g)
  state <- rep("S", N)
  state[sample(N, I0)] <- "I"

  # Precompute adjacency list for fast neighbor lookup
  adj <- igraph::as_adj_list(g)

  map_dfr(0:T, function(tt) {
    if (tt > 0) {
      infected_ids <- which(state == "I")

      # Collect newly infected nodes
      new_I <- integer(0)
      for (v in infected_ids) {
        nbrs        <- as.integer(adj[[v]])
        suscept_nbrs <- nbrs[state[nbrs] == "S"]
        if (length(suscept_nbrs) > 0) {
          newly  <- suscept_nbrs[rbinom(length(suscept_nbrs), 1, p_infect) == 1]
          new_I  <- c(new_I, newly)
        }
      }

      # Recovery
      recovering <- infected_ids[rbinom(length(infected_ids), 1, p_recover) == 1]

      # Update states — order matters: infections before recoveries
      state[unique(new_I)] <<- "I"
      state[recovering]    <<- "R"
    }

    tibble(
      t = tt,
      S = sum(state == "S"),
      I = sum(state == "I"),
      R = sum(state == "R")
    )
  })
}
```

```{r ch2-network-sir-run}
set.seed(2025)

# Run SIR on both networks with identical parameters
sir_er <- run_network_sir(g_er, I0 = 5, p_infect = 0.05, p_recover = 0.1,
                           T = 100, seed = 301)
sir_ba <- run_network_sir(g_ba, I0 = 5, p_infect = 0.05, p_recover = 0.1,
                           T = 100, seed = 302)

sir_network_df <- bind_rows(
  mutate(sir_er, network = "Erdős-Rényi"),
  mutate(sir_ba, network = "Barabási-Albert")
)
```

```{r ch2-network-sir-plot, fig.cap="SIR epidemic curves on two networks with the same mean degree. The Barabási-Albert scale-free network (right) produces faster initial spread through hubs, different peak timing, and a different final epidemic size than the structurally simpler Erdős-Rényi graph (left). The same transmission parameters; different interaction structures; different epidemics."}
sir_network_long <- sir_network_df %>%
  pivot_longer(c(S, I, R), names_to = "compartment", values_to = "count") %>%
  mutate(
    compartment = factor(compartment, levels = c("S", "I", "R"),
                         labels = c("susceptible", "infectious", "recovered"))
  )

ggplot(sir_network_long, aes(x = t, y = count, color = compartment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ network, labeller = label_both) +
  scale_color_manual(values = palette_ch2[c("susceptible", "infectious", "recovered")]) +
  labs(
    title    = "Network SIR: topology changes the epidemic",
    subtitle = paste0("Mean degree ~ ", round(mean_deg_er, 1),
                      " (ER) and ~ ", round(mean_deg_ba, 1), " (BA). Same parameters; different structure."),
    x        = "Time step",
    y        = "Count",
    color    = NULL
  )
```

```{r ch2-network-viz, fig.cap="Contact network structures at the peak of the epidemic. Node color indicates compartment status: blue = susceptible, red = infectious, green = recovered. Left: Erdős-Rényi graph, with roughly uniform degree distribution. Right: Barabási-Albert graph, with visible hub nodes carrying many connections. The hub structure changes the epidemic's geometry."}
set.seed(2025)

# Find peak time for each network
t_peak_er <- sir_er %>% filter(I == max(I)) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(t)
t_peak_ba <- sir_ba %>% filter(I == max(I)) %>% slice(1) %>% pull(t)

# Helper: get node states at a given time step
get_states_at_t <- function(g, t_target, I0 = 5, p_infect = 0.05,
                              p_recover = 0.1, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  N     <- igraph::vcount(g)
  state <- rep("S", N)
  state[sample(N, I0)] <- "I"
  adj   <- igraph::as_adj_list(g)

  for (tt in seq_len(t_target)) {
    infected_ids <- which(state == "I")
    new_I <- integer(0)
    for (v in infected_ids) {
      nbrs         <- as.integer(adj[[v]])
      suscept_nbrs <- nbrs[state[nbrs] == "S"]
      if (length(suscept_nbrs) > 0) {
        newly <- suscept_nbrs[rbinom(length(suscept_nbrs), 1, p_infect) == 1]
        new_I <- c(new_I, newly)
      }
    }
    recovering       <- infected_ids[rbinom(length(infected_ids), 1, p_recover) == 1]
    state[unique(new_I)] <- "I"
    state[recovering]    <- "R"
  }
  state
}

states_er <- get_states_at_t(g_er, t_peak_er, seed = 301)
states_ba <- get_states_at_t(g_ba, t_peak_ba, seed = 302)

# Tidygraph objects for ggraph
tg_er <- as_tbl_graph(g_er) %>%
  mutate(compartment = states_er,
         network     = "Erdős-Rényi")

tg_ba <- as_tbl_graph(g_ba) %>%
  mutate(compartment = states_ba,
         network     = "Barabási-Albert")

plot_network <- function(tg, title_str, t_peak) {
  ggraph(tg, layout = "fr") +
    geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.05, color = "#888888") +
    geom_node_point(aes(color = compartment), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_color_manual(
      values = c(S = "#2D5F8A", I = "#C0392B", R = "#27AE60"),
      labels = c(S = "susceptible", I = "infectious", R = "recovered"),
      name   = NULL
    ) +
    labs(title = title_str,
         subtitle = paste0("At peak infectious (t = ", t_peak, ")")) +
    theme_void(base_family = "Source Serif 4") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          plot.title = element_text(family = "Raleway", size = 12),
          plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#FAFAF7", color = NA))
}

p_er_net <- plot_network(tg_er, "Erdős-Rényi", t_peak_er)
p_ba_net <- plot_network(tg_ba, "Barabási-Albert", t_peak_ba)

p_er_net + p_ba_net
```

The same $\beta$. The same $\gamma$ and a different outcome.

The ODE has no state variable or parameter representing contact network topology [@PastorSatorras2001]. No values of $\beta$ and $\gamma$ reproduce the difference between these two epidemics — the model cannot distinguish Erdős-Rényi from Barabási-Albert contact structure except through changes in aggregate rates, and the aggregate rates are the same. In the model's terms, networks have no place to enter.

## The Reduction Principle {#sec-reduction}

The reduction principle is that familiar ODE models can be recovered as limits of appropriately constructed agent-based models. Agent homogeneity and mean-field contact structure are two central structural restrictions. Write each agent's property vector as $\theta_i = \theta_0 + \varepsilon_i$, and set $\varepsilon_i = 0$ for all $i$ — every agent is identical to the model's central reference parameter $\theta_0$. Then write the weighted contact matrix as $W = \bar{W} + \Delta W$, where $\bar{W}_{ij} = 1/(n-1)$ for $i \neq j$ and $\bar{W}_{ii} = 0$, and set $\Delta W = 0$. Under exchangeability and a fixed row total, $\bar W$ is the uniform contact baseline [@Jaynes1957]. A large-population ODE limit additionally requires compatible event-rate scaling and regularity conditions [@Kurtz1970; @Kurtz1978]. Population size alone says nothing about contact structure: increasing a lattice, household network, or scale-free network need not produce the well-mixed ODE.

The demonstration is direct. Fix a Barabási-Albert contact structure and scale up the population, holding all rate parameters constant. As $N$ grows, demographic stochasticity shrinks and the stochastic replicates collapse toward a single curve. That curve is not the ODE.

```{r ch2-lln-demo, fig.cap="The law of large numbers operating on a structured contact network. Each panel shows the infectious fraction $I(t)/N$ for eight stochastic replicates (blue) on a Barabási-Albert scale-free network at three population sizes. As $N$ increases, stochastic variation contracts and the replicates collapse toward a single trajectory. The ODE (dashed red) does not move: the converging trajectories approach the structured-network mean, not the mean-field limit. Large $N$ buys variance reduction. It does not correct structural bias."}
# LLN demonstration on a structured (BA) contact network.
# Population size increases; contact structure type is held fixed.
# Each BA network is generated fresh at each N with the same preferential-attachment
# rule (m = avg_deg/2), so the contact structure scales with the population
# but remains scale-free at every N.
# This chunk may take a minute on first render; results are cached.

set.seed(2025)

N_values_lln  <- c(300L, 1200L, 5000L)
n_reps_lln    <- 8L
avg_deg_lln   <- 6L
I0_frac_lln   <- 0.01   # 1% initial infected, constant across N

run_ba_sir_lln <- function(N, I0_frac = 0.01, p_infect = 0.05, p_recover = 0.1,
                            T = 100, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  I0    <- max(1L, round(I0_frac * N))
  g     <- igraph::sample_pa(N, m = avg_deg_lln %/% 2L, directed = FALSE)
  state <- rep("S", N)
  state[sample(N, I0)] <- "I"
  adj   <- igraph::as_adj_list(g)

  map_dfr(0:T, function(tt) {
    if (tt > 0) {
      infected_ids <- which(state == "I")
      new_I <- integer(0)
      for (v in infected_ids) {
        nbrs         <- as.integer(adj[[v]])
        suscept_nbrs <- nbrs[state[nbrs] == "S"]
        if (length(suscept_nbrs) > 0) {
          newly  <- suscept_nbrs[rbinom(length(suscept_nbrs), 1, p_infect) == 1]
          new_I  <- c(new_I, newly)
        }
      }
      recovering           <- infected_ids[rbinom(length(infected_ids), 1, p_recover) == 1]
      state[unique(new_I)] <<- "I"
      state[recovering]    <<- "R"
    }
    tibble(t = tt, I_frac = sum(state == "I") / N)
  })
}

lln_demo_runs <- map_dfr(N_values_lln, function(n_val) {
  map_dfr(seq_len(n_reps_lln), function(r) {
    run_ba_sir_lln(N = n_val, I0_frac = I0_frac_lln,
                   seed = 600L + n_val + r, T = 100) %>%
      mutate(N = n_val, rep = r)
  })
}) %>%
  mutate(N_label = factor(paste0("N = ", scales::comma(N)),
                          levels = paste0("N = ", scales::comma(sort(N_values_lln)))))

# ODE comparison in fraction formulation — does not depend on N.
# R0 = p_infect * avg_deg / p_recover = 0.05 * 6 / 0.1 = 3.
# Discrete-to-continuous correction: gamma = -log(1 - p_recover); beta = R0 * gamma.
gamma_lln <- -log(1 - 0.1)
beta_lln  <- 3 * gamma_lln

sir_frac_ode <- function(t, state, params) {
  with(as.list(c(state, params)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I
    dI <-  beta * S * I - gamma * I
    dR <-  gamma * I
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}

ode_lln_df <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(
  ode(y     = c(S = 1 - I0_frac_lln, I = I0_frac_lln, R = 0),
      times = seq(0, 100, by = 0.5),
      func  = sir_frac_ode,
      parms = c(beta = beta_lln, gamma = gamma_lln))
)) %>% rename(t = time)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = lln_demo_runs,
    aes(x = t, y = I_frac, group = interaction(N, rep)),
    alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.45, color = "#2D5F8A"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = ode_lln_df,
    aes(x = t, y = I),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "#C0392B", linewidth = 1.0
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ N_label, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title    = "Large N stabilizes trajectories — around the network mean, not the ODE",
    subtitle = paste0("BA network SIR, ", n_reps_lln, " replicates per N. ",
                      "Dashed: ODE (R\u2080 = 3). Noise vanishes; structural gap persists."),
    x        = "Time step",
    y        = "Infectious fraction (I / N)"
  )
```

The law of large numbers is doing its job. The variance is contracting with $N$ exactly as the theory requires. What it is not doing is closing the gap between the structured-network trajectory and the mean-field limit. The dashed ODE line sits persistently apart. The gap does not narrow with more replicates, and it does not narrow with larger $N$. It is the structural consequence of the contact network topology — and it persists because the network persists.

When data are recorded at coarse temporal resolution — weekly, quarterly, annually — the sequence of individual interactions within each observation interval is unobservable. Contacts that occurred in a specific order between specific agents are treated as simultaneous. Under exchangeability and a fixed contact total, uniform mixing is a symmetry-based baseline for this unresolved structure [@Jaynes1957]. It is not uniquely least-informative without those constraints. Structured models can still be compared when they imply distinguishable aggregate behavior at the observed frequency; otherwise the observation design does not identify the within-interval pairing and order. This resembles a sampling limit, though the Nyquist theorem applies specifically to regularly sampled, band-limited signals [-@Nyquist1928]. The resulting bias is the price of statistical stability under the chosen baseline.

The data constraint and the structural claim are not the same argument. The data constraint says: at this observation frequency, the data cannot distinguish mean-field from structured interaction. The structural claim says: the phenomenon's natural time scale is slow enough that interactions genuinely randomize between observations — that $\Delta W \approx 0$ is warranted by the system's dynamics, not merely forced by the data. The first is imposed by the observation design. The second is a philosophical contention about the phenomenon. A researcher with high-frequency contact data who nevertheless invokes the mean-field is making the structural claim. A researcher with only low-frequency data who invokes it may be making either — and should say which, because the two have different implications for what could, in principle, falsify the model.

One formal version of this principle appears in the theory of density-dependent Markov chains [@Kurtz1970; @Kurtz1978]: as $n \to \infty$, as $\varepsilon_i \to 0$ for all $i$, and as $\Delta W \to 0$, the ABM converges in distribution to the ODE. This is a conditional result: it says what the ABM becomes when both restrictions are imposed simultaneously. In that limiting case, the ODE is not an approximation to the ABM but the reduced form obtained after imposing the relevant restrictions. The question is always whether those restrictions are warranted for the phenomenon at hand.

The ABM is the richer language; the ODE is the sublanguage recovered under homogeneity and mean-field contact. They are related by named restrictions rather than by a vague appeal to complexity or realism. The ODEs are a singularity with the broader family. The choice between them is a question about which restrictions are warranted for the phenomenon and the data.

The ABM has more nominal parameters than the Lotka-Volterra ODE: $p_\text{birth}$, $p_\text{eat}$, $p_\text{death}$, the population size, the pairing mechanism. The ODE has four: $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\delta$, $\gamma$. A regression with a thousand predictors may have a sparse solution concentrated on ten — nominal and effective dimensionality are different things. The scientist who counts predictors before asking whether the signal is sparse has the analysis backwards. The critic who counts ABM parameters before asking how many degrees of freedom the dynamics of interest actually require has made the same mistake. Many regions of the ABM's parameter space produce qualitatively identical behavior — cycling statistically indistinguishable from the ODE output. The consequential structure — the boundary between cycling and extinction, the dependence of extinction probability on population size — is low-dimensional relative to the nominal parameter count. The ODE is the ABM under maximal regularization of both $\varepsilon_i$ and $\Delta W$: the restriction that produces its analytical tractability is the same restriction that removes certain phenomena from its vocabulary, and no amount of careful parameter estimation recovers what that regularization has discarded.

Parameterize the contact matrix as a mixture: with probability $p$, each infected agent contacts a random individual drawn uniformly from the population; with probability $1-p$, it contacts a neighbor from the scale-free network. At $p = 1$, $\Delta W = 0$ exactly — the mean-field. At $p = 0$, $\Delta W$ carries the full network structure. Every intermediate value is a point on the regularization path.

Each curve below is the mean of fifteen stochastic runs. The ODE is parameterized to match: $\gamma = -\log(1 - p_\text{recover})$ converts the ABM's geometric per-step recovery to its continuous-time equivalent, and $\beta$ is scaled to preserve $\mathcal{R}_0 = 3$ under that corrected $\gamma$. A residual gap between the $p = 1$ mean and the ODE dashed line is unavoidable — the ABM operates in discrete time with step size 1, while the ODE is continuous; at unit step size, higher-order discretization terms remain. The gap closes as the step size shrinks. It does not close with more data, more replicates, or better parameter tuning. It is not a calibration failure. It is the boundary between the two languages.

```{r ch2-regularization-path, fig.cap="The regularization path from structured network contact ($p = 0$, full $\\Delta W$) to random mixing ($p = 1$, $\\Delta W = 0$). Each curve shows $I(t)$ for a different value of the mixing probability on the Barabási-Albert network. The ODE (dashed) is the $p = 1$ limit. Dialing $p$ from 0 to 1 shrinks $\\Delta W$ toward zero: the regularization path between the structured ABM and the differential equation."}
set.seed(2025)  # reproducibility

# Mixed contact SIR: each infected agent makes contacts_per_step contacts per step.
# Each contact is drawn from the global population with probability p_random,
# or from the network neighborhood with probability 1 - p_random.
# Total contact rate is held constant across p_random values, so differences
# in dynamics are purely structural — a change in Delta W, not in contact rate.
run_mixed_sir <- function(g, p_random = 0.5, I0 = 5, p_infect = 0.05,
                           p_recover = 0.1, contacts_per_step = 6,
                           T = 100, seed = 42) {
  set.seed(seed)
  N     <- igraph::vcount(g)
  state <- rep("S", N)
  state[sample(N, I0)] <- "I"
  adj   <- igraph::as_adj_list(g)

  map_dfr(0:T, function(tt) {
    if (tt > 0) {
      infected_ids <- which(state == "I")
      new_I <- integer(0)

      for (v in infected_ids) {
        # Binomial split: n_rand contacts from global pool, remainder from network
        n_rand <- rbinom(1, contacts_per_step, p_random)
        n_net  <- contacts_per_step - n_rand

        contacts <- integer(0)
        if (n_rand > 0)
          contacts <- c(contacts,
                        sample(setdiff(seq_len(N), v), min(n_rand, N - 1),
                               replace = FALSE))
        if (n_net > 0) {
          nbrs <- as.integer(adj[[v]])
          if (length(nbrs) > 0)
            contacts <- c(contacts,
                          sample(nbrs, min(n_net, length(nbrs)), replace = FALSE))
        }

        suscept <- contacts[state[contacts] == "S"]
        if (length(suscept) > 0)
          new_I <- c(new_I, suscept[rbinom(length(suscept), 1, p_infect) == 1])
      }

      recovering           <- infected_ids[rbinom(length(infected_ids), 1, p_recover) == 1]
      state[unique(new_I)] <<- "I"
      state[recovering]    <<- "R"
    }
    tibble(t = tt, S = sum(state == "S"), I = sum(state == "I"), R = sum(state == "R"))
  })
}

# Five points on the regularization path — 15 replicates each, averaged to
# reduce stochastic noise so the p=1 mean converges visually to the ODE
p_values <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0)
n_reps   <- 15

mixed_runs <- map_dfr(seq_along(p_values), function(i) {
  map_dfr(seq_len(n_reps), function(r) {
    run_mixed_sir(g_ba, p_random = p_values[i], I0 = 5,
                  p_infect = 0.05, p_recover = 0.1, contacts_per_step = avg_deg,
                  T = 100, seed = 400 + (i - 1) * n_reps + r) %>%
      mutate(p_random = p_values[i])
  })
}) %>%
  group_by(p_random, t) %>%
  summarise(I = mean(I), .groups = "drop")

# ODE overlay. Discrete-to-continuous conversion must correct BOTH parameters
# jointly to preserve R0. The discrete ABM has R0_disc = p_infect * c / p_recover = 3.
# The exact continuous equivalents are:
#   gamma_cont = -log(1 - p_recover)              # geometric → exponential recovery
#   beta_cont  = R0_disc * gamma_cont / N         # preserves R0 = 3 in continuous ODE
# Using gamma=0.1 directly (without the correction) lowers the effective continuous
# R0 to 2.85 and shifts the ODE peak down; correcting only gamma without adjusting
# beta has the opposite effect. Correcting both holds R0=3.
gamma_reg <- -log(1 - 0.1)
beta_reg  <- 3 * gamma_reg / N_net
ode_reg  <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(
  ode(y     = c(S = N_net - 5, I = 5, R = 0),
      times = seq(0, 100, by = 0.5),
      func  = sir_ode_ch2,
      parms = c(beta = beta_reg, gamma = gamma_reg))
)) %>% rename(t = time)

ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = mixed_runs,
    aes(x = t, y = I, color = p_random, group = p_random),
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = ode_reg,
    aes(x = t, y = I),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "#1C1C1E", linewidth = 1.0
  ) +
  scale_color_gradient(
    low    = "#8A4A2D",
    high   = "#2D5F8A",
    name   = expression(p),
    breaks = p_values,
    labels = p_values
  ) +
  annotate("text", x = 80, y = max(ode_reg$I) * 1.05,
           label = "ODE (p = 1 limit)", family = "Source Serif 4",
           size = 3.2, color = "#1C1C1E", hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title    = "Regularization path: structured contact to mean-field",
    subtitle = paste0("BA network, N = ", N_net,
                      ". p = 1: random mixing. p = 0: network-only contact."),
    x        = "Time step",
    y        = "Infectious individuals (I)"
  )
```

## Wolf-Sheep Predation and the Absorbing Boundary {#sec-spatial}

> **Note for readers:** This section is not walked through in the live session. The pre-rendered animation and figures are shown as demonstration. The full implementation is distributed in `slides/render_spatial_anim.R` and `slides/render_parallel_runs.R`.

The predator-prey models introduced thus far preserve the mean-field assumption in one way: agents move randomly, and a wolf encounters any sheep with equal probability regardless of position. The spatial extension removes that last refuge of the ODE. A wolf eats a sheep only if they occupy the same cell on a $51 \times 51$ toroidal grid. Contact is local. Neighborhoods exist.

The model is a direct R translation of Wilensky's (2005) Wolf-Sheep Predation in NetLogo — a model with a thirty-year history of classroom use in complex systems courses. The rules are spare:

- Each tick, all agents perform a random walk to an adjacent cell.
- Wolves lose one energy unit per tick.
- A wolf on the same cell as one or more sheep grabs one at random, gaining `wolf_gain_food` energy. Each sheep can be eaten by at most one wolf per tick.
- Any agent whose energy falls below zero dies.
- Each agent reproduces with a small per-tick probability, halving its energy and placing an offspring in an adjacent cell.

The key line — the one that changes everything — is the spatial restriction on predation. In the random-mixing ABM, a wolf samples from the full population. Here it samples from `sheep-here`: sheep sharing its current cell. The mean-field assumption is gone.

```{r ch2-spatial-code, eval=FALSE}
# Wolf-Sheep Predation — R translation of Wilensky (2005) NetLogo model
# Full implementation: slides/render_spatial_anim.R
# set.seed(2025)

G             <- 51L   # 51x51 toroidal grid (NetLogo default)
wolf_gain_food <- 20L
sheep_reproduce <- 4.0   # % per tick
wolf_reproduce  <- 5.0   # % per tick

wrap <- function(v, g) ((v - 1L) %% g) + 1L

random_walk <- function(x, y, g) {
  dx <- sample(-1L:1L, length(x), replace = TRUE)
  dy <- sample(-1L:1L, length(y), replace = TRUE)
  list(x = wrap(x + dx, g), y = wrap(y + dy, g))
}

# Wolves eat one random sheep per cell; each sheep eaten at most once per tick
eats <- wolf_df |>
  left_join(sheep_df, by = c("x", "y"), relationship = "many-to-many") |>
  group_by(wolf_id)  |> slice_sample(n = 1L) |> ungroup() |>
  group_by(sheep_id) |> slice_sample(n = 1L) |> ungroup()
```

The animation below shows every tick of a single run from $t = 0$ to extinction at $t = 146$. Sheep (blue) expand freely in the early ticks. Wolves (red) follow with a lag, cluster where sheep are dense, and overshoot. By $t = 110$ the wolves number 544; only 195 sheep remain. The prey base collapses. The wolves, now hunting an empty grid, starve.

```{r ch2-spatial-anim, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Wolf-Sheep Predation on a 51×51 toroidal grid. Each frame is one tick; the animation runs from t = 0 to extinction at t = 146. Sheep: blue. Wolves: red.", out.width="55%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("../slides/spatial_lv.gif")
```

```{r ch2-spatial-ts, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Population time series for the same run. Wolf overshoot at $t \\approx 110$ depletes the prey base; both species reach zero by $t = 146$.", out.width="90%"}
knitr::include_graphics("../slides/wolf_sheep_timeseries.png")
```

The ODE with equivalent parameters cycles forever. The ABM does not necessarily or even usually. This is not a quantitative discrepancy — not a matter of the ABM predicting a slightly different amplitude or period. The finite stochastic population hits zero in finite time, after which extinction is absorbing. The deterministic ODE does represent zero as an invariant boundary, but a trajectory starting from positive populations does not hit that boundary in finite time. The distinction is between a state absent from the deterministic trajectory and a state absent from the equations themselves.

### The Stabilizing Role of Grass

One is entitled to ask whether extinction is the inevitable outcome or merely the typical one — and whether the ODE's cycling behavior could emerge from the ABM under different conditions. Both questions have the same answer: add grass.

The grass variant of the model (Wilensky 2005) introduces a third trophic level. Each grid cell is either green (grazeable) or brown (exhausted). A sheep on a green cell gains `sheep_gain_from_food` energy units, turning the cell brown. Brown cells regrow to green after `grass_regrowth_time` ticks. Sheep now lose one energy unit per tick regardless of predation — they must eat to live.

```{r ch2-grass-code, eval=FALSE}
# Grass extension — slides/render_parallel_runs.R
sheep_gain_from_food <- 4L
grass_regrowth_time  <- 30L

# patch_countdown is a flat integer vector of length G*G.
# 0 = green (grazeable); >0 = brown, counting down to regrowth.
cell_idx <- function(x, y, g) (x - 1L) * g + y

# Each tick: sheep on green patches eat; patch turns brown.
s_cells  <- cell_idx(agents$x[sheep_idx], agents$y[sheep_idx], G)
is_green <- patch_countdown[s_cells] == 0L
eat_df   <- tibble(row = sheep_idx[is_green], cell = s_cells[is_green]) |>
  group_by(cell) |> slice_sample(n = 1L) |> ungroup()
agents$energy[eat_df$row] <- agents$energy[eat_df$row] + sheep_gain_from_food
patch_countdown[eat_df$cell] <- grass_regrowth_time

# Each tick: brown patches count down.
patch_countdown[patch_countdown > 0L] <- patch_countdown[patch_countdown > 0L] - 1L
```

The mechanism is a resource cycle. When sheep are scarce, ungrazed patches recover. Recovered grass feeds surviving sheep. A recovering sheep population eventually supports a recovering wolf population. The feedback is negative at every link: high wolves $\rightarrow$ low sheep $\rightarrow$ grass recovery $\rightarrow$ sheep recovery $\rightarrow$ wolf recovery. This is the structure that generates sustained oscillation.

The question is empirical. Fifty independent runs of each variant, 300 ticks each:

```{r ch2-parallel-runs, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="50 independent runs of the no-grass (left) and grass (right) Wolf-Sheep models, 300 ticks each. Without grass, 47 of 50 runs end in wolf overshoot and sheep extinction. With grass, 49 of 50 runs sustain both populations to t = 300.", out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("../slides/parallel_runs.png")
```

Without grass, 47 of 50 runs end in wolf overshoot followed by sheep extinction. Cycling is the exception — three runs in fifty. With grass, 49 of 50 runs sustain both species to $t = 300$. The third trophic level converts extinction from the norm to the anomaly.

This result exposes something about the ODE that the ODE itself cannot reveal. The Lotka-Volterra prey equation is:

$$\frac{dN}{dt} = \alpha N - \beta NP$$

The $\alpha N$ term says prey grow at a fixed per-capita rate, limited only by predation. This is not an approximation of a world with unlimited grass. It *is* a world with unlimited grass, encoded in functional form. The structural assumption is not stated.

The grass model makes the assumption explicit, then relaxes it. When grass is finite and regrows slowly, the prey's recovery mechanism is bounded. Wolf overshoot can exhaust both prey and prey's food supply simultaneously, leaving the system with no path back from low sheep numbers. The absorbing boundary becomes reachable.

The ODE cycles forever not because cyclic dynamics are general — the ABM shows they are not — but because inexhaustible prey resources are built into this model's structure. In probabilistic terms, that fixed structural choice can be represented as a degenerate prior on the resource specification. It is a strong claim about the world, stated implicitly in the functional form; whether it is warranted depends on the system being modeled.
